rules.title: Consonants Change with Position
rules.explanation: ㄱ, ㄷ, ㅂ, and ㅈ sound close to a soft English k, t, p, and ch at the start of a word. Once they land between two vowels, the vocal cords start vibrating earlier and they soften toward g, d, b, and j instead. It's the same letter — position just changes how hard or soft it lands.

examples.note: the first ㅂ starts the word (softer p); the one after a vowel softens toward b
father — ㅂ between vowels sounds close to b
meat — the second ㄱ, between vowels, softens toward g

rules.title: ㅅ Becomes "sh" Before 이 or a Y-Vowel
rules.explanation: ㅅ is normally a plain s sound, but right before the vowel ㅣ or a y-glide vowel (야, 여, 요, 유), it shifts to an sh sound instead.

rules.title: Final Consonants Collapse to 7 Sounds
rules.explanation: Korean can end a syllable with many different consonant letters, but when spoken they all collapse into just seven sounds: [k], [n], [t], [l], [m], [p], and [ng]. Several letters share an ending sound — ㄷ, ㅅ, ㅈ, ㅊ, ㅌ, and ㅎ are all pronounced [t] at the end of a syllable.

rules.title: A Final ㅎ Disappears Before a Vowel
rules.explanation: When a syllable ending in ㅎ is followed by a syllable that starts with a vowel, the ㅎ isn't pronounced at all — the two syllables just blend together.

rules.title: A Final Consonant Slides Into the Next Syllable
rules.explanation: When a syllable's final consonant is followed by a syllable starting with the silent placeholder ㅇ, that consonant's sound slides over and becomes the start of the next syllable. The spelling doesn't change — only how it's spoken.

examples.note: food (+ subject marker) — the ㄱ of 식 slides onto 이
the Korean language — the ㄱ of 국 slides onto 어

rules.title: ㅂ/ㄷ/ㄱ Soften Before ㅁ or ㄴ
rules.explanation: When a syllable ending in a ㅂ-type, ㄷ-type, or ㄱ-type sound is immediately followed by a syllable starting with ㅁ or ㄴ, that final sound turns nasal — ㅂ becomes ㅁ, ㄷ becomes ㄴ, and ㄱ becomes ㅇ.

examples.note: the Korean language — ㄱ before ㅁ becomes [ㅇ]
is / am / are (formal) — ㅂ before ㄴ becomes [ㅁ]

rules.title: ㅎ Fuses With a Neighbor Into an Aspirated Sound
rules.explanation: ㅎ tends to disappear into whichever plain consonant sits next to it, fusing with ㄱ, ㄷ, ㅂ, or ㅈ to produce the matching aspirated (extra-breathy) sound: ㅋ, ㅌ, ㅍ, or ㅊ.

examples.note: to be good — ㅎ + ㄷ → 타
to be many — ㅎ + ㄷ → 타

rules.title: Aspirated Consonants: ㅋ ㅌ ㅍ ㅊ
rules.explanation: These four are the "breathy" partners of ㄱ, ㄷ, ㅂ, and ㅈ — said with a noticeably stronger puff of air, closer to how English says k, t, p, and ch at the start of a stressed word.

rules.title: Tensed Consonants: ㄲ ㄸ ㅃ ㅆ ㅉ
rules.explanation: These five are pronounced with the throat tightened and almost no puff of air released — a harder, more clipped version of ㄱ, ㄷ, ㅂ, ㅅ, and ㅈ. A quick self-check: hold a thin strip of paper in front of your mouth — it should barely move for a tensed consonant, versus a lot for an aspirated one.

rules.title: Some Plain Consonants Get Tensed Automatically
rules.explanation: When ㄱ, ㄷ, ㅂ, ㅅ, or ㅈ starts a syllable right after certain final consonants, it automatically hardens into its tensed version — even though the spelling stays plain.

rules.title: The Six "W-Glide" Compound Vowels
rules.explanation: 와, 워, 왜, 웨, 외, and 위 are all built the same way: start with your lips rounded as if to say ㅗ or ㅜ, then glide quickly into the second vowel. 외 ends up sounding just like 웨.

rules.title: ㅢ Changes Depending on Where It Falls
rules.explanation: ㅢ keeps its full sound only when it's the very first syllable of a word. As a later syllable it's easiest to say as [이], and if a consonant is written in front of it, it's pronounced simply as [이] too.

examples.note: doctor — first syllable, keeps its full sound
